rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Remark 6.9 paragraph 2, line 440 [8d2fca9 numbering]
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-derived from scratch (line 440 changed). With A_n the event that some look among the first n rejects (Proposition 6.1), A_n is contained in A_{n+1}, so an added look can only add rejections, with extra probability P(A_{n+1} minus A_n). For normal data that difference contains the open set {|S_t| < b_t for t <= n, |S_{n+1}| > b_{n+1}} for any finite positive boundaries b_t: it is nonempty (y_1 = ... = y_n = 0, y_{n+1} = 2 b_{n+1}) and the density of (Y_1, ..., Y_{n+1}) is positive everywhere, so the probability is positive. A design whose rejection probability already equals alpha (all of alpha spent) therefore exceeds alpha when the look is added. The paragraph states the qualifiers 'for normal data' and 'a design that has spent all of alpha'. Sanity check by simulation (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/extralook.py, 2,000,000 normal null paths, seed 9): a constant two-sided boundary c = 2.4119 on |Z_t| over 5 looks calibrated to total size 0.05000; adding a sixth look at the same boundary raises the rejection probability to 0.05532 (+0.0053), i.e. above alpha, as the argument says. The two numbers in the paragraph are in L01-num-rem69. rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: New displayed result since 9b6be31, re-derived. Claim: with h = 1/alpha, h P0(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) + E0[sum_{k<=n} (M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] <= 1. Derivation: Theorem 6.4's proof gives E0[W_n] <= 1 with W_n = sum_k M_k 1_{A_k} + M_n 1_{B_n}; drop the nonnegative term M_n 1_{B_n} and write M_k = h + (M_k - h) on A_k. Sound. Second claim: the expected overshoot O_n = E0[sum_{k<=n}(M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] is nondecreasing in n because every summand is >= 0 (M_k >= h on A_k); it is positive from the first day n_0 with P(A_{n_0}) > 0 because M_{n_0} > h almost surely on A_{n_0} (shown in the previous sentence for the monitor); so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= (1 - O_n)/h = alpha (1 - O_n) <= alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) for n >= n_0, and letting n grow (monotone limit) the probability of ever crossing is at most alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) < alpha. Sound; for this monitor n_0 = 1 and the gap is tiny in absolute terms but strictly positive, and the sentence claims only 'strictly below alpha'. Numerical spot-check (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify8-L01-L02/overshoot.py, 40,000 null paths of the monitor with alpha = 0.05, kappa = 252, horizon 2520): P(cross) = 0.0199 < 0.05, E[overshoot] = 0.0191 > 0, h P + O = 0.417 <= E[W_n] = 0.989 <= 1. Notation: h, M_k, A_k, B_k and 'the same steps' refer to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which the sentence names; A_n of Proposition 6.1's proof is a different, proof-local event, so there is no collision inside either proof. rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Round-8 FAIL, re-checked from scratch at 3dd9a69 (line 440 changed in 9a7195b). The page now reads: 'Within its budget a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks can be cheap, as O'Brien and Fleming's power finding above illustrates. A spending design's guarantee also ends with its budget, though.' This is exactly the round-8 proposed replacement. Re-judged on its own merits. (1) Support: the evidence for 'can be cheap' is the B span on line 439 (O'Brien and Fleming, Abstract). I re-read the abstract (OpenAlex, curl 2026-10-19, no email, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/dl/oa_10_2307_2530245.json): 'comparing two treatments when response to treatment is both dichotomous ... and immediate ... The maximum number (N) of tests and the number (m1 + m2) of observations collected between successive tests is fixed in advance. The overall size of the procedure is shown to be controlled with virtually the same accuracy as the single sample chi-square test ... The power is also found to be virtually the same.' That is a fixed-number-of-looks design, so a power finding about it supports a statement about 'a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks', and 'can be cheap' is existential and says 'illustrates', not 'all such designs are'. (2) The second sentence moved to 'a spending design' (Lan and DeMets); its support is not the O'Brien-Fleming finding but the page's own argument two sentences later (nested events as in Proposition 6.1, positive probability by part (b), so a design that has spent all of alpha exceeds alpha once an uncovered look is added), which I re-derived (see L01-math-rem69-extralook). The Lan-DeMets abstract (OpenAlex, same date, dl/oa_10_1093_biomet_70_3_659.json) says the boundary 'is determined by alpha*(t), and by past and current decision times, but does not depend on the future decision times or the total number of decision times': a spending design is flexible about the number and timing of looks inside its budget and has no alpha left beyond it, which is what 'ends with its budget' says. (3) Consistency with the rest of the page, re-read: line 439 ('Pocock ... O'Brien and Fleming fix the maximum number of tests ... Lan and DeMets ... replace it with a function alpha*(t)'), quiz item 14's explanation ('Pocock and O'Brien-Fleming fix the number of looks in advance; Lan and DeMets free their number and timing but still spend a fixed alpha'), key-results row 13 and card S7-c146 all separate fixed-look designs from spending designs the same way. The generalization from a fixed-look design's power to 'a spending design' is gone. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Set-up' and 'Construction' (lines 437-440)
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-derived. m' = m - i + 1 true nulls, c = min(c_i, 1/m'). Since alpha < 1 and c_i > alpha/m' we have c > alpha/m' (both c_i and 1/m' exceed alpha/m'), so m'c > alpha. Construction: i - 1 false nulls at p-value 0 (a false null's p-value is unconstrained; validity is required only of true nulls), true nulls q_j = (U + (j-1)/m') mod 1 for U uniform on [0,1): each q_j is uniform (rotation of the circle), hence valid (P(q_j <= u) = u). Assumptions complete: alpha in (0,1), positive constants, any other constants. The device is the one of Problem P2 (p_2 = (U + 1/2) mod 1), as the page says. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'A false rejection' (lines 443-445)
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-derived. Almost surely every q_j > 0 (q_j = 0 only for one value of U), so the i - 1 zeros are p_(1) = ... = p_(i-1) = 0 and p_(i) = min_j q_j belongs to a true null. Zeros pass steps 1, ..., i - 1 because the constants are positive (the step fails only when p_(k) > c_k). If min_j q_j <= c <= c_i, step i passes, so the first failing index is > i and H_(i), a true null, is rejected. Hence FWER >= P(min q <= c) = m'c = min(m' c_i, 1) > alpha (m' c_i > alpha by hypothesis, 1 > alpha). The page states it as an inequality; the equality FWER = min(m' c_i, 1) also holds (step i is then decisive: it passes iff min q <= c_i, and the arcs of length c_i cover the circle when c_i >= 1/m'), which I confirmed numerically; the lesson does not need it. [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Zeros are a convenience' (line 448)
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-derived. False-null p-values in (0, delta] with delta <= c_j for all j < i: on {delta < min_j q_j <= c} the i - 1 smallest p-values are the false nulls' (each <= delta <= its constant, so steps 1..i-1 pass) and p_(i) = min q <= c <= c_i passes, so a true null is rejected. For delta <= c, P(delta < min q <= c) = m'(c - delta) because the arcs of length delta (<= c <= 1/m') are also disjoint; it exceeds alpha iff delta < c - alpha/m'. The claim is a lower bound on the FWER, as written ('exceeds alpha once delta < c - alpha/m''). Simulated (400 random cases, random m <= 8, random i, random other constants, random false-null p-values in (0, delta]): the estimated FWER was never below m'(c - delta) - 1e-3 and was above alpha whenever delta < c - alpha/m' - 1e-3 (0 violations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'What it shows' (line 449)
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Checked sentence by sentence. (1) 'A step-down procedure with fixed constants that controls the FWER at level alpha under every joint distribution of valid p-values must have c_k <= alpha/(m + 1 - k) for every k': the contrapositive of the main result (positive constants, alpha < 1). (2) 'Raising constants only adds rejections, because the first failure moves later, so Holm's procedure rejects everything such a procedure rejects, for every vector of p-values': if c_k <= Holm_k for all k then p_(k) > Holm_k implies p_(k) > c_k, so the first failing index of the c-procedure is no later than Holm's and it rejects a subset. (3) 'A gain beyond Holm's needs the dependence between the tests (Lessons 4 and 5)': true for the class the problem treats (p-value step-down with fixed constants, every configuration of true nulls possible, only marginal validity). Outside that class gains can come from logical relations between the hypotheses (Shaffer 1986) as well as from dependence; the sentence is a pointer, sits after the sentence that fixes the class, and is not a graded claim span. Note, not a failure. (4) The T span after it matches Lehmann and Romano Theorem 2.3(ii) (L02-cite-lehmann2005generalizations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 88 (new figcaption sentence)
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: New sentence: 'testing each hypothesis at α/m holds the family-wise error rate at or below α for every m, and here, with independent nulls, at exactly α only when m = 1.' Derivation: by Boole's inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2), the FWER of m true nulls each tested at α/m is at most m·(α/m) = α for any dependence, so 'at or below α for every m' holds. With independent true nulls, FWER = 1 − (1 − α/m)^m. Bernoulli's inequality (1 − x)^m ≥ 1 − mx holds with strict inequality for m ≥ 2 and 0 < x < 1, so FWER < α for m ≥ 2; at m = 1 the FWER is exactly α. Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, .venv): for α = 0.01..0.10 and m = 1..200, 500, 1000, 5000: 0 violations of FWER ≤ α; strictly below α for every m ≥ 2; |FWER − α| ≤ 1e-15 at m = 1. Values: α = 0.05: FWER(2) = 0.049375, FWER(1000) = 0.048772; α = 0.01: FWER(1000) = 0.009950. The figure's readout and desc in every state agree (row L02-fig-fwer-growth). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421, the shifted construction
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-derived at 535fd80 with s = alpha/2 and p2 = (U + s) mod 1. For U in [0, 1 - s): p2 = U + s > s, so p2 <= s only at U = 0 (p2 = s). For U in [1 - s, 1): p2 = U + s - 1 in [0, s), so p2 <= s. Hence {p2 <= s} = {0} u [1 - s, 1) (exact on the 160000-point rational grid: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 2, 'A2 equals {0} u [1 - alpha/2, 1) on the grid: True'). Since s < 1 - s for alpha < 1, {U <= s} n {p2 <= s} = {0}, a null set. P(A1) = P(A2) = s, P(A1 n A2) = 0, so P(union) = 2s = alpha. The text 'which meets {U <= alpha/2} only at the null point U = 0, so the two events are disjoint up to a null set and the FWER is again exactly alpha' is TRUE. Monte Carlo: section 3 (mean over 20 seeds of 1,000,000 draws: 0.050002 +- 0.000035). Round-15 FAIL (L02-math-P2-shift-disjoint PASS in round 15) re-checked and still PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421 ('E[U((U+s) mod 1)] = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 ... correlation 1 - 6s(1-s)')
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Derivation at 535fd80. V = (U + s) mod 1 equals U + s on [0, 1-s) and U + s - 1 on [1-s, 1]. E[UV] = int_0^{1-s} u(u+s) du + int_{1-s}^1 u(u+s-1) du = [(1-s)^3/3 + s(1-s)^2/2] + [1/3 - (1-s)/2 + (1-s)^3/6] = (1-s)^2/2 + 1/3 - (1-s)/2 = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 (using (1-s)^3/2 + s(1-s)^2/2 = (1-s)^2/2 and (1-s)^2/2 - (1-s)/2 = -s(1-s)/2). With E U = E V = 1/2 and Var U = Var V = 1/12 (V uniform), Cov = 1/12 - s(1-s)/2 and corr = 12 Cov = 1 - 6s(1-s). Numerical check: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 1 evaluates both identities with Fraction arithmetic at 28 rational shifts (k/13, k/97, 1/2, 1/40, 1/20, 1/10, 3/7, 1/4, 2/9, 7/11): both hold exactly at every point (printed: 'points tested: 28'). E[UV] and corr are polynomials of degree at most 3 in s, so 28 exact agreements cover the family. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html section 7, bullet 2 (line 448): 'a 50-day versus a 55-day lookback, which share 50 of their 55 days, can be highly correlated' [8d2fca9 numbering]

So 'can be highly correlated' is supported by a computed case under i.i.d. returns, and the sentence claims only that the case is possible. PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129 (the paragraph after Example 2.4), first sentence: 'The bound in (1) is attained when the true-null p-values are uniform and their rejection events {p_i <= alpha/m} are pairwise disjoint up to a null set (Problem P2)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since e968af2 (git diff checked); round-19 evidence: Re-checked at 45fff85 (line 129 changed: 'disjoint' became 'disjoint up to a null set'). Proof: P(union A_i) = sum_i P(A_i minus union_{j<i} A_j), and P(A_i minus ...) = P(A_i) iff P(A_i and A_j) = 0 for every j < i; so Boole's inequality is an equality iff the pairwise intersections are null (the 'up to a null set' qualifier is exactly right). With uniform true-null p-values, P(p_i <= alpha/m) = alpha/m, so FWER = m0 alpha/m. Construction (P2, exact check p2_p4_exact.out): p1 = U, p2 = (U + alpha/2) mod 1 gives P(A) = P(B) = alpha/2, P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = alpha exactly (alpha = 1/20). Sufficiency is shown; the sentence's 'attained when' is a sufficient condition, which is what it claims.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html section 8 key-results table, row 8 (line 530; grade B; cite romano2005stepwise)
rows.evidence: RE-CHECKED FROM SCRATCH at ad9d3e1 (round-19 FAIL: 'with more power than single-step methods' asserted an unqualified advantage). The row now reads 'A stepwise bootstrap procedure exploiting dependence controls the FWER asymptotically and often rejects more false hypotheses than single-step methods' (grade B). (1) Publisher record: Crossref 10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00615.x (curl, no identifying parameter; scratch downloads/romano/crossref_romano.json): 'Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping', Econometrica 73(4) 1237-1282, July 2005 (= registry). (2) Published abstract: the Econometric Society page for the article (https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/2005/07/01/stepwise-multiple-testing-formalized-data-snooping, HTTP 200; scratch downloads/romano/es_romano.html), quoted: 'This paper suggests a stepwise multiple testing procedure that asymptotically controls the familywise error rate. Compared to related single-step methods, the procedure is more powerful and often will reject more false hypotheses. ... Unlike some stepwise methods, the method implicitly captures the joint dependence structure of the test statistics ...'. IDEAS (scratch downloads/romano/ideas_romano.html, meta description, 'Copyright The Econometric Society 2005') gives the same sentences. (3) Author copy of the published article (M. Wolf's UZH publications page links etca.pdf; 46 pp.; header 'Econometrica, Vol. 73, No. 4 (July, 2005), 1237-1282'; text at scratch downloads/romano/romano_wolf_2005_etca.txt): keywords 'Bootstrap, data snooping, familywise error, multiple testing, stepwise method'; Algorithm 3.2 computes the critical values 'via the bootstrap'; Theorem 3.1(ii): 'The method asymptotically controls the FWE at level alpha; that is, lim_T FWEP <= alpha'; Section 3 (p. 1246): 'The stepwise procedure is therefore more powerful than the single-step method. Nevertheless, the stepwise procedure still asymptotically controls the FWE at level alpha'; Remark 3.1: 'One consequence is that often more false null hypotheses are rejected. Clearly, this is an advantage, resulting in improved power.' Each element of row 8 is supported: stepwise (yes), bootstrap (keyword; Algorithm 3.2), exploiting dependence (joint dependence captured), controls the FWER asymptotically (Theorem 3.1(ii)), often rejects more false hypotheses than single-step methods (abstract; Remark 3.1). The 'often' hedge matches the paper. Grade B (BLUEPRINT 3: published in a top journal; the power claim is hedged and not contested by a named source, see L01-L02-counter-romano2005stepwise-e968af2). The row carries no quotation, so no data-locator is needed.
